rows: In plain English
Precise wording
**Cut the grocery tax; raise income taxes**
No GET on groceries; raise all income-tax rates by the same percentage
**Cut the grocery tax; trim a low-income credit**
No GET on groceries; cut the food/excise tax credit
**Tax profit from selling assets like regular income; cut top rates**
Tax long-term capital gains like regular income; lower the top three income-tax rates
**Raise the top rate to cut low rates or boost a credit**
Raise the top income-tax rate by 1 point; lower the bottom three rates, or enlarge the food/excise credit
**Stop taxing profit from selling assets; raise top rates**
Exempt long-term capital gains from tax; raise the top three income-tax rates
**Raise the sales tax (GET) a little; cut income taxes**
Raise the GET rate by half a point; lower all income-tax rates by the same percentage
Chapter
What the draft finds
In the draft
**2 · Individual income tax**

Higher earners pay a larger share of their income in Hawaiʻi's individual income tax, which brought in $3.29 billion in fiscal 2025, and Act 24 adds a 13 percent top rate above $500,000 for single filers (pp. 3, 28, 35).
[pp. 26–55](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=28)
**3 · General excise tax**

The general excise tax is the state's largest, at $4.63 billion or 40.4 percent of fiscal 2025 collections, and because it applies to sales between businesses it can pile up at each stage of production (pp. 3, 56, 60).
[pp. 56–72](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=58)
**4 · Visitors and tourism**

Taxing visitors can help residents, but only if residents are paid back for the share they also pay; the hotel and vacation-rental tax, for example, raised $816.2 million in fiscal 2025 (pp. 73–74, 77).
[pp. 73–85](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=75)
**5 · Property and real estate**

Hawaiʻi homeowners pay 0.29 percent of their home value in property tax, the lowest rate of the 50 states and well below the 0.90 percent national figure, and only the counties may set it (pp. 87–88).
[pp. 86–99](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=88)
**6 · Business taxes**

The corporate income tax raised $400.4 million net in fiscal 2025, and UHERO says a large rate cut could raise total revenue once the effects on other taxes are counted, although that rests on 2010 data (pp. 101, 107).
[pp. 100–117](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=102)
**7 · Wealth and estates**

UHERO considers an annual wealth tax unlikely to raise much revenue if Hawaiʻi acts alone, while estate tax collections swing widely, reaching $405.8 million in fiscal 2025 including a one-time $315 million payment (pp. 118, 120).
[pp. 118–132](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=120)
**8 · Tax credits**
Credits work like spending, and taxpayers claimed $621.3 million of them in 2023, while 72 percent of what individuals claimed in solar credits went to filers earning $100,000 or more (pp. 133, 147).
[pp. 133–156](https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/stats/trc/docs2025/2026-10-08_UHERO_draft_report.pdf#page=135)
